### BOOK ONE.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, holding a book or tablet within a rectangular frame with floral/scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>

ACCORDING to the Platonists and the Hebrews <note>The author is likely referring to Kabbalistic scholars, as he mentions the mystical power of names.</note>, the knowledge of the Divine names is not lowly, but sublime. The Hebrews valued this science so much that they placed it not only before all other sciences, but even before the written law <note>The written law refers to the Torah, the first five books of the Bible.</note> itself. They asserted that this knowledge was given to the patriarchs and to Moses; to Moses, it was given not through dead writing, but as something planted within his mind, and so passed on successively to the prophets, and ultimately to those who succeeded them. By the virtue of these names, the Hebrews say their ancestors performed marvelous things. Regarding these names, the ancients spoke in many places, though not complete—

# MIRROR OF SALVATION
## OF THE NAME OF JESUS.
### BY THE REVEREND FATHER FRIAR ARCANGELO
->From Borgonovo Piacentino, of the<-
->Friars Minor of the Observance <note>The Friars Minor of the Observance were a branch of the Franciscan Order that sought a stricter, more traditional adherence to the Rule of Saint Francis.</note>.<-

### BOOK ONE.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a reclining figure, possibly a saint or biblical figure, in a landscape setting with foliage.</image-desc>

According to the Platonists <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Plato; during the Renaissance, many Christian scholars integrated Platonic ideas about the soul and the divine into their theology.</note> and the Hebrews <note>Referring here to Jewish mystical traditions, particularly the Kabbalah, which explores the hidden meanings of the names of God.</note>, the knowledge of the Divine names is not lowly, but sublime. The Hebrews esteemed this science so highly that they placed it not only before all other sciences, but even before the written law itself, affirming that it had been given to the patriarchs and to Moses. To Moses, it was given not through dead writing <note>A reference to the idea that the "spirit" or mystical understanding of the law is living, whereas the literal text alone can be "dead" without its divine interpretation.</note>, but was implanted within his mind, and so passed successively to the prophets, and ultimately to those who succeeded them. Through the power of these names, the Hebrews say, their ancestors performed marvelous things; regarding these names, those ancients spoke in many places, though not completely— <note>The Italian text ends mid-word with "compitamẽ-", likely intended to be "completamente" (completely).</note>

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Book One, introducing the "Mirror of Salvation" and establishing the mystical importance of Divine names as a tradition passed from Moses to the prophets.</summary>
<keywords>Mirror of Salvation, Name of Jesus, Arcangelo da Borgonovo, Divine names, Moses, Platonism, Hebrew tradition, Kabbalah</keywords>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, which discussed the transmission of the secret knowledge of Divine names from Moses through the prophets, this page focuses on the specific power of the Tetragrammaton and the Name of Jesus, citing the Church Father Origen to justify why these names should remain in their original Hebrew form.</meta>

### BOOK I.
A
<meta>catchword: born</meta>

...tely, but separately; not clearly, but obscurely. If anyone knows how to gather, recognize, and pronounce these names with such purity of mind, directed toward those effects for which they are intended, he is powerful enough to perform great things. This is particularly true regarding the first name of God, which is pronounced with four letters <note>original: יהוה — the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God often rendered as YHWH or Yahweh.</note>, all of which are vowels <note>During the Renaissance, many Christian Hebraists argued that the letters of the Tetragrammaton functioned as vowels to emphasize its spiritual, breath-like nature.</note>. This most holy name is to be pronounced by no one—except by one who is full of the spirit, with right intention, and for a legitimate cause—according to the Hebrews, because they are compelled to confess that JESUS <note>original: ישו (Yeshu)</note>, whom they call the Nazarene, is a divine name. 

Origen <note>An influential early Christian theologian (c. 185–253 AD) who studied the relationship between Greek philosophy and Hebrew scripture.</note>, having considered the marvelous power <term>virtù|In this context, 'virtue' refers to an inherent, miraculous power or efficacy rather than just moral goodness.</term> of the divine names in his book *Against Celsus*, said: "In certain divine and sacred names there lies hidden a wonderful power; therefore, they are not to be translated from Hebrew into a foreign language, but are to be preserved in their own characters." This is perhaps because, just as in the human body life remains stable through a certain logic of composition—which, if changed or altered, would cause that life to cease—so the Hebrews believe that in divine names composed according to Hebrew custom, there exists a certain vital power, just as he had previously taug—

<note>divine names, יהוה (YHWH), JESUS, ישו (Yeshu), Origen, Celsus, Hebrew, power</note>

<summary>This page explains the mystical power of the Tetragrammaton and the Name of Jesus, arguing that divine names possess an inherent "vital virtue" that is lost if they are translated out of their original Hebrew characters.</summary>
<keywords>Tetragrammaton, Name of Jesus, Origen, Against Celsus, Hebrew mysticism, linguistic theology, sacred languages, Renaissance Hebraism</keywords>

### BOOK I.
A ij

...born Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure portrayed as a combination of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with writing the Hermetic corpus.</note>, and many after him: Plotinus, and Iamblichus <note>original: "statio" — this word is unclear; it may be a corruption of "citato" (cited) or a reference to a specific school or location.</note>: who say that with those names, uttered in the manner described, the Demons <note>In this Neoplatonic context, 'Demons' (daimones) refers to intermediary spirits or supernatural entities that inhabit the air, rather than purely evil beings.</note> are conquered. And this: through God's providence, whenever the need arises, we may rightly use them, invoking help from them. They say that this was first used and observed by Pythagoras, of whom they say that with certain divine words he cured some of many infirmities, both of the soul and of the body. We find this same way of proceeding in the wisdom of Zoroaster: which Plato calls divine in the *Alcibiades* <note>The *Alcibiades I*, a Socratic dialogue, discusses the "magic" of Zoroaster as being the true worship of the gods.</note>. No one should marvel at such <term>power|virtù: In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the 'occult' or inherent efficacy of a thing to produce a specific effect.</term> hidden in divine names if they consider this natural power: when we see knowledge descend from the object to the sense, and from the senses to the imagination, and from this to the mind; and from the mind, the first concept is conceived, then, almost as if by way of childbirth, it is expressed by means of the voice. Therefore, in this voice, formed of its various parts, the power of the thing remains hidden under the form of meanings. This power, or life, first originates from the mind through the seeds of things <note>The "seminal reasons" (logoi spermatikoi), a concept suggesting that the rational blueprints for all things exist within the divine mind.</note>, then is brought forth by the voice, and ultimately is preserved through writing. Wherefore, if all names include within themselves a certain power...

<summary>This page explores the Neoplatonic and Hermetic belief that divine names possess inherent power (virtù) used by sages like Pythagoras and Zoroaster to heal and command spirits. It explains that this power flows from the mind into the voice and finally into writing.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Plotinus, Iamblichus, Pythagoras, Zoroaster, Plato, divine names, virtù, philosophy of language, demons, spiritual healing</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument that divine names are not arbitrary labels but contain the actual essence and power of the things they signify. It builds on the previous discussion of how concepts move from the mind to the voice.</meta>

### BOOK I.
A
<meta>catchword: in the power of [original: penes]</meta>

...and through that [voice], almost as if through an image of things, those things are known. Much more so will the names given by God perpetually <note>original: "ppetuo"</note> preserve their <term>power|virtù: In this context, it refers to the inherent, active efficacy or spiritual essence within a name.</term>, and this not without merit: because a true name (as Plato pleases) is nothing other than a power of the signified thing, first conceived <note>original: "cõcetta"</note> by the mind <note>original: "mēte"</note> (as we have said), then expressed by the voice, and ultimately <note>original: "ultimamēte"</note> signified through <note>original: "p"</note> letters. Because, to signify a divine thing, it is necessary that the name include within itself the divine power: therefore (the power being in divine names), Plato in the *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue by Plato regarding the soul; here the author references the sacredness of names as vessels of truth.</note> commands that they be honored and revered more than divine statues. This is because the expression of the image of God is more manifest in the artistry of a mind especially <note>original: "massimamēte"</note> inspired by God than in that which is reserved for the works <note>original: "ope"</note> of human hands. 

But Plato judges that the first and most sincere names of God exist within the celestial <note>original: "supne" (superne)</note> minds: by whom God is more expressly (if it is permitted to say so) conceived <note>original: "cõceputo"</note> and understood; then in the purest Demons <note>In the Neoplatonic sense, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil.</note>; and finally <note>original: "ultimamēte"</note> in the souls of men. And these souls, when they are good, are showered with the influence of God; and then these names are uttered as if from trumpets <note>original: "trōbe"</note>. The divine names, therefore, <note>original: "adūque"</note> given to us by the holy men of ancient times, appear to be the image and rays of God, *in the power of* <note>original: "penes" — this is a catchword leading into the next page.</note>

**Plato, Phaedo, divine names, power, image of God, Demons, divine influence**

<summary>The text argues that divine names possess inherent spiritual power because they are products of divine inspiration in the mind rather than mere human handiwork. It describes a hierarchy where these names descend from celestial minds to pure spirits and finally to the souls of holy men.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Phaedo, divine names, occult power, Neoplatonism, divine inspiration, celestial hierarchy, intermediate spirits</keywords>

## BOOK II.
->A iii<-

...enlightening <note>The Italian text begins with the suffix "-rante," likely the conclusion of a word such as *illustrante* (enlightening) or *instaurante* (restoring) from the previous page.</note> the minds of men through the superior deities <note>original: "numi superiori," referring to divine powers or gods</note>, everyone who sees the sun, or anything similar to it, reveres it and its light. In the same way, it is first necessary to adore God through His rays: which are the virtues <term>virtues|virtù: spiritual powers or inherent efficacies</term> and images hidden within the meaning of the sacred names. For this reason, Socrates in the *Philebus* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of pleasure and the good life.</note> cries out in this way: "There was always within me a reverence toward the divine and sacred names"; and he was not led to this by a certain human fear, but by love, which surpasses every great fear. Let us hear Plato in the eleventh book of the *Laws*, who says: "Those who defile the divine names of the Gods through lies or perjury deserve to be punished by everyone without exception <note>original: "sanza nota di punitione," literally "without a mark of punishment," likely meaning punishment should be swift and certain without further legal record or delay</note>; and whoever is present and does not punish them ought himself to be punished as a transgressor of the law." We should not be troubled if we have heard the name of "many Gods" from Plato; because in the *Parmenides* and in the *Timaeus*, he proves that there is only one God, while the others he names as Angels and God's celestial ministers. Therefore, when he names the "Gods," he intends not only the [actual] Gods but also divine men. And after Plato in the *Parmenides* compared all things to the one God, he judged that for this reason those names should not be despised; because a wonderful power being hidden in these names, not undeservedly <note>The text ends mid-word with "imerita-", the start of *imeritamente* (undeservedly).</note>...

### BOOK I.

...to be weeded <note>original: "runcati," referring to the goddess Patelana mentioned on the previous page, who presided over the opening of the husks or the weeding of the fields</note>, that is, cut from the earth, according to **Varro**. **Spinensis** was worshiped as a God, so that he might root out the thorns from the fields, as **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo</note> affirms. **Nemestrinus** was the God of groves and forests, as **Arnobius** says. ...no: <note>The text begins with the fragment "ue," likely the conclusion of the name "Giunone" (Juno) or a reference to her as Jove's spouse from the previous page.</note> who was also named (according to **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note>) **Lucina** <note>original: "Lucina", from *lux* (light); the goddess who brings the newborn into the light</note> and **Diana**, in the belief that she gave light to men. She was called **Egeria**: because women believed they were helped by her in their childbirth. Beyond this, she was named **Iuga**: because she was joined in marriage with **Jove**; and for this reason, it was believed that she favored those who wished to marry. For this same reason, she was also called **Interduca** and **Domiduca** by the Romans: believing that she accompanied the bride all the way to the husband's house. She was called **Socigena** (according to **Martianus** <note>Martianus Capella, a late antique author</note>) because she accompanied the groom, uniting him with the bride. She was called **Popolana**: because (as Martianus says) she was worshipped by the people. She was called Great Juno, Queen Juno, **Moneta** <note>The "Warner" or "Advisor"</note>, **Sospita** <note>The "Savior" or "Deliverer"</note>, **Matuta** <note>Goddess of the dawn and birth</note>, **Novella**, **Calendare** <note>Referring to the Kalends, the first of the month, which were sacred to Juno</note>: and she was called by other almost innumerable names.

**Saturn** was the son of **Caelus** <note>The personification of the Sky or Heavens</note>, as **Lactantius** writes. **Orpheus** gives many praises to this Saturn in his hymnary, naming him unpolluted, uncontaminated, a God of great strength, and the prince of generation <note>The source of all creation or procreation</note>; he has also been called an "investigator" <note>original: "investigatore"</note> by **Virgil**. **Rhea**, who is called **Cybele**, was the mother of the Gods (according to **Strabo**) and was the wife of Saturn. She was called **Dindymene** <note>A title derived from Mount Dindymus, a site of her cult</note>, according to **Catullus**.

...of the forests: but also of all material things. **Fortuna** <note>The Roman goddess of luck and fate</note> was a Goddess; of whom **Juvenal** <note>A Roman poet of the late 1st century AD</note>, speaking, said: "We make you a Goddess, **Fortuna**, and place you in heaven." <note>original Latin: "Te facimus Fortuna Deam caeloque locamus"</note> The **Philosophers** concluded this Goddess to have been blind and mad; and there were many other Gods among the **Gentiles** <term>gentiles: in this context, the non-Christian peoples of antiquity</term>, whom we shall omit for the sake of brevity.

**F. A.** My Lord, it was not without a good purpose that I have expanded somewhat in naming these Gods. The reason has been so that everyone might know how blind the world was, and caught in the darkness of ignorance, until such time as the true light was born—the one who has illuminated the whole world (and that is **Jesus Christ**) —so that everyone might run to the light of the knowledge of this light, Jesus, just as he himself testified, saying: "I am the light of the world; while you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be children of light." <note>original Latin: "Ego sum lux mundi, dum lucem habetis, credite in lucem, ut filii lucis sitis"</note> Because if you leave this light, you walk through the darkness not knowing where you are going. Thus, Your Lordship can see that I have not done this without cause; but if it pleases you that I proceed further regarding these Gods to satisfy you, I will gladly do so.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of causality and how we name God based on His effects. It follows the previous page’s introduction of naming God through "remotion" (what He is not) and begins to explain how names are applied through the relationship between a cause and its effect.</meta>

-># BOOK I.<-

...[by] another disposition added by nature: such an effect will also have a likeness to this cause; and similarly, the cause will have a likeness to such an effect. Whence the **builder** is the cause of the house, not according to his nature but according to his **art**; therefore, the likeness of the house is not in the nature of the builder, but in his art. 

Furthermore, since the **good** has the character of an **end** <term>end: (Latin: *finis*) the purpose or goal for which something exists or is done; the "final cause" in Aristotelian philosophy.</term>, and because the good is desired by all, the end is the first cause of all four causes <note>The four causes of Aristotle: Material (what it's made of), Formal (its shape/essence), Efficient (who made it), and Final (its purpose).</note>. The **good** is that to which the character of causing primarily belongs; therefore, the primacy of the cause shall be according to the perfection of the good. 

So it is that since **God** is the **supreme good**—not by **participation** <term>participation: the philosophical idea that created things "take part" in a quality (like goodness or beauty) that God possesses perfectly and essentially.</term> but according to His very being—He is the cause of every existing thing. Therefore, in Him shall be the likeness of all His effects; and thus every cause can be named by the names of its effects. 

For if this likeness exists according to an identity of nature, that name will befit both the cause and the thing caused, just as the name "man" befits both the generator and the generated <note>original: *generante* and *generato*; referring to a father and his child sharing the same human nature.</note>. But if there is no likeness according to that same species, but the cause is instead more preeminent, the name will not be common to the one and the other according to the same reasoning:

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 23 regarding the divine names and how one should approach the study of Holy Scripture. It transitions from a list of attributes to a philosophical explanation of how God is named through both "affirmative" and "negative" theology.</meta>

-># BOOK I.<-

At their first approach to divine readings, they must bow their knees and, with reverence and fear, enter with a purified mind into the contemplation <term>Contemplation: A deep, prayerful focus on divine truths, moving beyond simple reasoning to a direct "gazing" upon the mystery of God.</term> of them; for by doing so, they will undoubtedly be among those who are enlightened. It is true that those names which do not signify some beneficial effect of God within us do not appear as clearly in the aforementioned sacred scriptures—as, for example, *infinite*, *immense*, *invisible*, *dwelling in inaccessible light*, and other similar **negative names** <note>original: "nomi negatiui." This refers to "Apophatic theology," which defines God by what He is not (e.g., "infinite" means "not finite") to emphasize His transcendence.</note>. However, He is found through His **affirmative names** by means of a secret **analogy** <term>Analogy: In theology, the use of earthly terms to describe God. For example, calling God "Father" is an analogy that uses a human relationship to hint at a divine reality that is far greater.</term>, or through property, proportion, suitability, or likeness. This occurs in the "excellence of negation," because of a super-excellence that surpasses everything. Thus, just as He is in His creatures, so too does God—dwelling in many hearts—form His names within them, naming and manifesting Himself to those people. For this reason, to name oneself is nothing other than to declare oneself. Therefore, let all divine names, both affirmative and negative (the latter of which far exceed the affirmative), be forever blessed.

# BOOK I.

I say, then, that Being is more universal than anything else and is self-evident, and yet it requires explanation. Thus, we define its parts as follows:

**The Great** <note>original: "Magnum."</note> is that Being by virtue of which all things are great; and magnitude does not attach to the great unless the great performs great works. This is because, in whatever degree a perfection is understood and known—which degree is nonetheless a degree of that specific perfection—the formal essence of that perfection is not removed because of it.

Thus, if one wished to define the thing that includes, the thing included "formally" would be the definition, or part of the definition, of the includer. Because if the definition of truth in general does not have wisdom within itself, then infinite truth likewise does not have infinite wisdom within itself. Therefore, there is a certain "formal non-identity" between wisdom and goodness, insofar as there would be distinct definitions for them if they were definable.

However, a definition demonstrates not only the <term>quiddity</term><note>From the Latin *quidditas*, literally the "what-ness" of a thing; its essential nature or what makes it what it is.</note> produced by the intellect, but the real quiddity as well. Therefore, among these attributes, there is no "formal identity" in their real existence. By this I mean to say: that when the intellect joins these together—[for example,] that "wisdom is not goodness formally"—it does not create the truth of this composition through its own act of comparison. Rather, it finds these extremes already present in the object; the true act of the mind is formed from the combination of these [pre-existing] elements. 

The ancient doctors spoke of this argument regarding "non-formal identity," positing that <note>original: "in diuinis"</note> in divine matters, there is such a thing as <term>predication</term><note>The act of declaring or "predicating" a quality of a subject, such as saying "God is good."</note> that is true by identity, but which is nonetheless not "formally" true. Thus, through identity, truth is goodness in reality.

**S. T.** What is this "formality" of which you have told me so much? It seems to me that the entire power of concluding that there are diverse attributes in God depends on this.

**F. A.** My dear S., a formality is that thing which, when added to another, changes the <term>reason</term><note>Here, "reason" refers to the "formal reason" or the defining concept of a thing—what makes it what it is.</note> of the thing being formed. This is clearly seen in God and His intellect: for God is called "intelligent" because of His intellect, and not because of His will; but He is called "willing" <note>original: "volens"</note> because of His will. This is what Plato says in the *Timaeus*: goodness is the <term>idea</term><note>In the Platonic sense, an "Idea" or "Form" is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing.</note> of the good, just as <term>entity</term><note>The quality of being or existing.</note> is the idea of the being, and unity is the idea of the one. Thus, the "Good" exists because of "goodness," and the "Being" exists because of "entity." 

This "formality" is distinct from a "mode": because a mode (even though it is added to something else) does not change the essential reason of the thing formed. Examples of modes include finitude, contingency, and existence. Thus, all men are called "finite," yet it is not because of a formality called "finitude" [that they are men]; nor are they called "existent" because of "existence" [as a separate definition], but rather by their own proper formal reasons <note>The argument here is that while "Goodness" is a distinct concept that makes God good, "Existence" is just a mode of being and doesn't change the basic definition of what a thing is.</note>.

Therefore, just as all these perfections or attributes are the same thing within the divine essence, so too is one predicated of the other. For this proposition is true: *goodness is greatness*; and likewise *goodness is eternity*; *goodness is will*, and so on. This is because these attributes are essentially the same thing through a reciprocal identity, for they are all **formally infinite**. Because of this infinity, one is the same thing as the other. 

And this is the reason why (according to Augustine in the seventh book of *The Trinity*) the identity of the **Deity** and **paternity**<note>In Trinitarian theology, "Deity" refers to the shared divine nature, while "paternity" refers to the specific relational property of the Father. Augustine argues they are distinct in relation but one in substance.</note> is denied; for the Deity and paternity are not the same thing in the manner described above, because...

# BOOK I.

...one of them, that is, **paternity**<note>The state or quality of being a father; in this context, the specific relational property of the first person of the Trinity.</note>, is not **formally infinite**<note>To be "formally infinite" means to be infinite by its very definition or nature. The author argues that while God's nature is infinite, the specific role of "being a father" is a relation, not the totality of the infinite essence itself.</note>. For if it were so, the Father would be greater than the Son, because he would possess a formally infinite paternity which the Son would not possess. However, the **Deity** is formally infinite, and through this infinity, paternity is identified with it; but the reverse is not true. 

Thus, the aforementioned attributes are identified in such a way that this predication is verified: God is good by that same principle through which He is wise, *eodem*<note>original: "eodem" — Latin for "by the same."</note>, that is, as if by mutual identity. Wherefore the Deity, by that same simple essence, through the perfection of one and the same reason, is good, wise, eternal, and so forth. 

It is not the same, however, for "God" and "Father"; for neither the one nor the other is an essential perfection of that to which they are applied. Therefore, the following does not hold: *this is the same as another; therefore, it is formally the same as that same thing*<note>original: "questo e' idem alteri: ergo est formaliter idem eidem" — a logical principle being tested here regarding how different names for God relate to one another.</note>. Between goodness and wisdom there is true **identity**, because they are identified within the **essence**, without one being included in the definition of the other.

# BOOK I.

God, compared to those things which are imperfect and weak, is called perfection and form, because He is the author of every form and perfection. Yet, when compared to things that are perfect and beautiful <note>original: *formose*, implying both beauty and the possession of a defined "form"</note>, He is neither perfection nor form; this is because He possesses these not through the same properties that belong to those things, but in a way that is vastly different—or rather, higher by an infinite distance. Thus, He is said to be above every form and perfection that could ever be found or even conceived by us.

Therefore, just as time is the measure of fleeting things <note>original: *flussibili*, referring to objects in a state of flux or change</note>, so eternity <term>eternity: The original term is *evo* (from the Latin *aevum*), which in Renaissance philosophy often denotes the duration of unchanging, created things (like angels), serving as a middle ground between the "time" of the physical world and the "absolute eternity" of God.</term> is the measure of those things that [stably] exist. I call it an "adequate measure," just as time is adequate to fleeting things. God, therefore, when compared to fleeting things, is called eternity <note>original: *evo*</note>, because He—the sole Good superior to all beings—is not equal to all beings. This is because each of these beings <note>original: *enti*</note> is led back to its own principle <note>original: *prencipio*, meaning its source or foundational cause</note>, which is various and distinct from the others, as if it were its own.

And these such principles are reduced to one immense principle, which is a principle above every principle, giving order to each of them. This is because He measures the order of things under those principles, and He measures those principles under Himself; and therefore, every principle is beneath Him, for they receive that gift from Him. That which has, or is capable of, motion and change is called a natural principle; and the intellect that is superior to this mobile state can be called supernatural. This unity is termed the "unity of mind." God is superior even to this: wherefore He is called supernatural and super-essential <term>super-essential: translated from *supereffentiale* (super-essentialis). In Renaissance theology, this describes God as being "beyond essence" or "above being," meaning He does not exist in the way created things do but is the source of existence itself.</term>. He possesses these two dignities by a certain supernatural and super-essential reason. 

Every created essence (whether it be angelic or rational) possesses that unity which is super-essential. Because it possesses this within its essence, it rightfully holds the property of being "essential"—which is, nonetheless, above the mundane essence—but because it holds these qualities within its essence, it bears the name of the "essential." It also possesses the gift of the supernatural intellect, but with a certain natural condition: for it holds this within a mutable essence and power. Therefore, God alone possesses this supernatural and super-essential excellence, while created beings do not. It is just as the clear air possesses a truly shining light, whereas the cloudy air possesses the air itself, but not the brightness.

# BOOK II.

<note>original: "דיין"</note> *Dayan*, which means "judge," and <note>original: "צדיק"</note> *Zadic*, which means "just," and <note>original: "חנון"</note> *Channun*, which means "gracious" or "merciful," and others like them—all these are names common to both God and his creatures, and they are derived from other meanings. This is just as our masters affirm, speaking as if in the voice of God, saying: "My name is one, and uniquely appropriate to me, but the other names of God signify qualities." Because the names of the Creator have been multiplied, being derived from his various works, many of the sons of Adam <note>A traditional phrase referring to all of humanity.</note> have come to believe that God possesses many different qualities.

# BOOK II.

...and, "he shall call," <note>original Latin: *vocabit*</note> is written with those same letters and almost the same vowel points: the first, which is the passive form, is written thus וַיִּקָּרָא <note>original Hebrew: *vayiqqare*</note>, which means "he shall be named" or "called" <gloss>named</gloss>. The second, which is the active form, is written thus וַיִּקְרָא <note>original Hebrew: *vayyiqra*</note> with some changes in the points <note>The "points" refer to the niqqud, the vowel signs added to the Hebrew alphabet to indicate pronunciation and grammatical mood.</note>, and means for us, "he shall call" or "he shall ask." 

Let the Jews read the translation of the Seventy Hebrew interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, which tradition says was translated by 72 Jewish scholars in Alexandria.</note>, most learned men, in whom they place much faith—so much so that no one has ever dared to contradict them. These men translate the text of Isaiah in this way: **"A child is born to us, and a son is given to us, whose government is upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel."** <note>original Latin: *Puer natus est nobis, & filius datus est nobis, cuius imperium super humerum eius, & vocabitur nomen eius magni cōsilij Angelus.* The title "Angel of Great Counsel" is a distinct feature of the Septuagint's version of this verse.</note> 

And from this it appears manifestly that the text says *vayiqqare*, that is, "he shall be named," and not *vayyiqra*, that is, "he shall call." <meta>This page continues the explanation of the Hebrew verse from Isaiah (42:8) mentioned on the previous page: "I am the Lord, that is my name." The author is delving into the mystical grammar of the word "Hu" (He) to explain God's "naked" or absolute nature before He "clothes" Himself in attributes.</meta>

"Which is," <note>original: "quod est"</note> **He who is, is my name**: because that Hebrew word <note>original: "הוא"</note> *Hu* is not a referring relative pronoun—that is, "this one"—but is a word signifying **Himself** <note>original: "ipsum"</note>; that is, what He is, and supremely "this," meaning this One, who in this manner communicates Himself to no one. Wherefore it follows in the prophet: *My glory I will not give to another*: that is, that glory which I have in my supreme unity. 

Therefore, in no way (according to Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century mystical philosopher who taught that God is "super-essential" and beyond all human description.</note>) should we presume to comprehend that supreme unity and ineffable substance; which neither sense, nor imagination, nor speech, nor touch, nor our science can reach. For it is an unnamable, super-named, and **super-substantial deity**, withdrawn into its most remote recess of divinity and solitary retreat: hidden in the abyss of its darkness, and beyond that, remote from every relation, motion, deliberation, name, word, intellect, placement, or state—all of which are totally incompatible with our cognition.

...this essence; that within this unity there exists a plurality of deities <note>original: "numi"; referring to divine powers or manifestations</note>, to believe this is no error: for they are like rays that gush forth from the essence. These rays the philosophers called the "Gods of the nations"; the learned Hebrews called them "numerations," **Middot** <term>Middot (Hebrew: מִדּוֹת), meaning "measures" or "attributes," used in Kabbalah to describe the qualities of God.</term>, and **Sephiroth** <term>Sephiroth (Hebrew: סְפִירוֹת), the ten emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</term>. We call them "attributes" (as **Agrippa** <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), an influential theologian and occult writer who synthesized Kabbalah with Western philosophy.</note> cites). Orpheus, Pallas, and Mercury represent "intelligence"; Saturn represents the "fashioning of forms"; Neptune, "productive power"; Juno, the "nature of secret things"; Venus, "love and a lucid life"; and Apollo, "reason and the concept of the universe," and is called the "soul" insofar as he generates inferior things.

In this way, those most prudent theologians of the heathens, under various names and deities, and under a variety of genders, worshipped one single God. This God (as **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author who argued in his Natural History that human frailty divided the singular divine into various personifications.</note> says) fragile and toiling mortality divided into many Gods; being mindful of its own fragility, it did so in such a way that each person took that part which seemed necessary to them. Wherefore, if anyone desired faith, they worshipped Jove; whoever wanted prudence, Apollo; whoever wisdom, Minerva; and those who had need of other things invoked Him by other names. Therefore, to achieve a multiplicity of graces, they multiplied the attributes or deities of God; but God is one, upon whom everything depends.

Here, then, is placed the name of **Eheye**, a substantive verb in the indicative mood, including the three different tenses; therefore this divine name **Eheye** <note>original: אהיה</note> is interpreted as: I was, I am, and I shall be <note>original Latin: "fui, sum, & ero"</note>. For the second letter, called **He** <note>original: ה</note>, and the third, that is **Iod** <note>original: י</note>, of that name, signify the third person of the verb among the Hebrews, which for us is the first person of the past tense, which is pronounced **Hayiti** <note>original: הייתי; the text uses "hagiti," likely a transcription or printing error for the Hebrew past tense of "to be"</note>, meaning "I was," or "I have been." 

The fourth letter of that same name, that is, **He** <note>original: ה</note>, signifies the first person of the indicative which is called **Hoveh** <note>original: הוה</note>, meaning "I am." But the first letter, that is, **Aleph** <note>original: א</note>, which is usually placed at the beginning of the future tense for every verb—being a <term>servile letter</term> <note>a technical grammatical term for letters used as prefixes or suffixes to change a word's tense or function</note> of the future tense—signifies the first person of the future of that same verb. From this it is manifest that this name **Eheye** contains within itself the distinction of the three tenses of the indicative of the substantive verb—

The second thing to be noted is that in this tradition it is said: that the Holy and Blessed God, and his house of judgment, "made man" <note>original Latin: *fecerunt hominem*, using the plural form of the verb "to make."</note>. # BOOK II.

...four letters as well: which the Jews pronounce instead of the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The sacred four-letter name of God (YHWH), which is not spoken aloud in Jewish tradition.</note>, and it is called **Adonai** <note>Hebrew: אדני</note>. Through this name, the divine **Trinity** is also demonstrated, albeit in an indistinct <note>original: *confusamente*</note> manner. And just as **Elohim** <note>Hebrew: אלהים; a name for God that is grammatically plural in Hebrew.</note> implies plurality, so likewise **Adonai** is a plural name. This is because its singular form is **Adon** <note>Hebrew: אדון</note> and it signifies "the Lord"; its plural form is **Adonim** <note>Hebrew: אדנים</note> and it signifies "the Lords." From this singular name **Adon** is formed **Adoni** <note>Hebrew: אדוני</note>, which is interpreted as "my Lord"; and from this plural **Adonim** is formed **Adonai**, which is a Divine name and signifies "my Lord" <note>While the suffix implies a plural "my Lords," it is used as a singular title of majesty for God.</note>. 

Therefore, those ancient Fathers, instructed by **Moses**, ordained that God should be named by a word in the plural number to demonstrate that universal Dominion resides in the three Divine persons; for the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord. Thus, Lordship is common to all three persons. And to demonstrate that these three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are not three Gods, nor three Lords, but one single dominion common to all three, it was determined that the name **Adonai** (even though it is of the plural number) should not be joined <note>The text likely continues to explain that it is joined to a singular verb, emphasizing unity.</note>

**S. T.** What is meant by this "acquired name" of God, or a name outside of Him?

**F. A.** By the "acquired name" of God, and [a name] outside of Him, is understood all of our knowledge that we have of God, acquired through those works that appear and are manifest. Therefore, all that knowledge which is acquired of God from His works is called the "name of God." As much of God is known as His outward works manifest Him. Through the works, then, that God performs outside of Himself, the knowledge of God is generated in the hearts of men: [this is] reputation and fame; that is, the name of God acquired among men. Thus, a "good name" acquired is the knowledge, fame, estimation, or reputation with praise and honor acquired and generated in the hearts of men concerning someone. Just as, on the contrary, a "bad name" is the knowledge, fame, or estimation with reproach <note>original: "vituperio"; implies a sense of shame, disgrace, or verbal abuse.</note> and contempt acquired by someone in the hearts of men. A person has as much of a name as they have fame, reputation, and estimation in the hearts of others. And he who has no reputation or estimation has no name among men: because a person is honored by men only as much as they are known.

I say, therefore, that the name (according to the wise) is nothing other than the concept of the soul: which is made manifest through the voice, which voice explains the said concept, or word. Wherefore, just as the intellectual word <term>Intellectual word: In Scholastic philosophy, this is the "verbum mentis" or the internal thought before it is spoken aloud.</term> of man, in order that it may be manifested outwardly—that is, so that the concept of the mind may be revealed—it is necessary that it be made into a name and clothe itself in articulate voice; for otherwise the thing would only be known and manifest to the thinking person themselves.

In like manner, so that God might make manifest to us the Word <term>Word: Translating the Italian "verbo," referring to the Greek *Logos*, the second person of the Trinity.</term> and His Son, and the sacrament <note>Here "sacrament" is used in its older sense of a sacred mystery or hidden divine plan.</note> of His will, according to His good pleasure, He made that same Word—clothed in our humanity—into a Name. Through this Name (according to Paul) the most merciful Father has spoken to us in these final days.

And for this reason, we say that God has two names: the first, by which He names Himself and His consubstantial <term>Consubstantial: Sharing the same divine essence or substance; a key concept in the Nicene Creed describing the relationship between the Father and the Son.</term> Word. This Word, insofar as it is spoken by the Father from eternity <note>original: "ab eterno"</note>, is called the concept, through which the Father defines Himself. But insofar as it is the Word made flesh <note>original: "fatto carne"</note> and a Name, through it the Father has manifested Himself to us in time. The other name of God is vocal, uttered with the tongue, or written: with which God [is addressed] by us by His proper title...

### BOOK III.

consonant does not produce a sound by itself, because it cannot be a perfect part of a <term>dittione: a word or utterance</term> without an attached vowel: but it is joined with the vowel, and is therefore called a "consonant"—that is, *sounding together* <note>original: "insieme sonare"</note>—because only then can it be pronounced. Two consonants in a name, then, signify the humanity of **Christ** in one person, which humanity results from two things: namely, from the soul and the body. **Christ** in truth had true humanity, and consequently true flesh and a true soul. And the reason is that, just as the consonant does not sound by itself—that is, it cannot be a syllable—so the soul does not sound by itself, or does not signify a person; likewise, neither does the body signify such a person. 

Even if all the consonants are placed together, they do not sound—that is, they do not signify anything, nor can they be pronounced—but when joined with the vowels, they immediately produce sound. In the same way, the soul and the flesh of **Christ** do not constitute a person [on their own] in **Christ**: because [if they did] they would make two persons in **Christ**—namely, the human person constituted by these two aforementioned parts, and the divine person. But when these two parts, soul and body, are joined and united with the divinity, they are called one person: because the divine person removes from that composition of the soul and the body the power of the p-

And therefore this blessed name contains within itself all the parts of **grammar**. And I say that this glorious name is a **verb**: "In the beginning was the Word" <note>original Latin: "In principio erat verbum" (John 1:1). The author plays on the dual meaning of "verbum" as both a grammatical 'verb' and the theological 'Word' of God.</note>. It is a **participle**, because it takes the part of the noun—that is, human nature, but not the sin—and it takes part of the verb—that is, the person and the glory <note>In traditional grammar, a participle "participates" in both noun and verb qualities. The author uses this to explain the Incarnation, where Christ "participates" in both humanity and divinity.</note>. Beyond this, it is an **adverb**, because it makes man stand assumed <term>assunto: taken up or joined</term> near the divine Word in that same <term>supposito: a technical term for the 'hypostasis' or underlying personhood of Christ</term>. It is an **interjection**, because it interposes itself (as a faithful mediator) between God and man. It is a **conjunction**, because it joins the highest to the lowest: God to the mud, the Word to man, virginity to marriage, and the one fallen into misery to the glory of the highest God.

This name is glorious in heaven, on earth, and in hell, according to Philippians, chapter 2: "At the name of **JESUS** every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and in the lower parts" <note>Philippians 2:10</note>. # BOOK III.

And **Plutarch** <note>Plutarch (c. 46–119 AD) was a Greek philosopher and priest at Delphi. The author is referring to his essay *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*, where Plutarch explores why the ancient prophetic shrines were falling silent.</note> in the book of the same title says: "When I said to **Cleobrotus**, 'Tell me, oh friend (if it pleases you), for what reason have the oracles, about which you told so many marvelous things, become extinct?'" And Plutarch added: a voice was heard coming from the **Echinades Islands** <note>A group of islands in the Ionian Sea, off the coast of Acarnania.</note> at the time when **Christ** suffered, saying: "**The Great Pan is dead**" <note>This famous story from Plutarch tells of a sailor named Thamus who heard a divine voice announcing the death of "The Great Pan." While Pan was the Greek god of the wild, Christian theologians like the author of this manuscript interpreted "Pan" (which means "All" in Greek) as a symbol for the totality of the pagan world or the "all-powerful" demons, whose power ended at the moment of the Crucifixion.</note>; that is to say, his power was extinguished, both in ruling and in giving responses. And the fact that such a voice was heard was spread by public report even to **Tiberius Caesar**, who, having examined the witnesses, had this account placed in the royal archives. 

Thus the most famous **Delphic oracle** ceased; the **Pythian** <note>Another name for the Delphic oracle, associated with the dragon Python slain by Apollo.</note> also ceased, and all the others. And shortly after the death of **CHRIST the Warrior**, the temples of the gods were destroyed—such as those of **Apollo**, **Jupiter**, **Juno**, **Minerva**, **Diana**, and every false god—and temples were erected to **CHRIST**, and in honor of those who followed Him. So that we may rightly sing, saying:

->Behold, our God Christ reigns through the ages.<-

# BOOK III.

...we boast in the wind of mere words.

**F. A.** No human creature, nor angelic **S.**, nor any other, even if they all joined together, can perform any miracle, even the smallest. This is because every created thing is of finite and determined power; hence **Aristotle** in his *Categories* <term>original: "predicamenti"; refers to Aristotle's work on the classification of things</term> considered this statement impossible, saying: *From privation to possession, return is impossible* <note>original Latin: "A privatione ad habitum, impossibilis est regressus"</note>. An infinite distance exists between these two extremes—that is, between privation and the possession of a form—to which no created and limited thing can reach. Only God, therefore, is the worker of miracles. Thus, every miracle performed by a man—provided its substance is known to be true and not imaginary—whether it be great, mediocre, or small, must always be attributed to glorious God, if the order of sacred things has been observed. He is the only one who, either by Himself alone or through His delegate (yet never without Himself or the one substituted by Him), performs such things. The singer of the Holy Spirit <note>Referring to King David as the author of the Psalms</note> places this in Psalm 71: *Blessed be the Lord God, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things* <note>original Hebrew: ברוך יהוה אלהים אלהי ישראל עשה נפלאות לבדו (Baruch Adonai Elohim Elohei Yisrael oseh niflaot levado)</note>. If He alone does this, then creatures do not; therefore, God does this either by Himself or through His creatures. Hence the masters of law say: *What one does through oneself, one does through another in one's name...* <note>original Latin: "Quod quisque per se, id per alium suo nomi[ne]"</note>

<meta>catchword: Quod</meta>

<summary>F.A. argues that miracles are impossible for any created being, human or angelic, because their power is finite. He cites Aristotle and the Psalms to demonstrate that only God possesses the infinite power required to perform true wonders, whether directly or through an agent.</summary>

# BOOK III.

...can do, and this is confirmed by **Paul**, who says, *We are God’s fellow workers* <note>original Latin: "Cooperatores sumus Dei"; from 1 Corinthians 3:9</note>. We, therefore, are not those who perform miracles, but Almighty God: whom we confess alone does marvelous things: because His mercy is eternal. Piety, then, mercy, beneficence, and grace are the cause of such operations—not force, nor rigor, nor finally any debt or obligation. The purpose of miracles is confession, magnificence, glory, honor, and worship: of which the God of gods, and the Lord of lords, is worthy. Let us confess, then, that He is good. 

No rule is assigned by any philosopher, however learned, that can persuade us of the true art from which the will of the Gods must necessarily follow—whether that rule consists of specific words, or is bound by certain symbols <term>original: "caratteri"; refers here to magical sigils or occult signs</term>—since it belongs to Him who binds and commands to rule, and not to be ruled: because He is greater than all. A creature, then, cannot perform miracles unless it is united with the Divinity through fervor; by means of this union, it is not we ourselves acting as God, but God acting through us as His friends—wishing to show us favor—who performs miracles.

This is just as God also said to Moses in Exodus, chapter 3: "I am who I am" (or "I will do what I will do," as we have seen above), "thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you." He spoke this way to demonstrate that perfect being resides in Him—or rather, that the being of God is infinite and His very own.

...that grace granted to Christ as man is not infinite, but is called "full": because it is found in him according to every variety of its effects. It is as if someone were as white as it is possible to be white; such a person would be said to have "whiteness without measure." It is also described this way in respect to the capacity of the soul: for example, if someone were to go to a river and fill a vessel to its maximum capacity, he would be said to have taken water "without measure," even though the vessel itself has a determined size. ### BOOK IV.

->GG iii)<-

**Athanasius** <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373), a prominent Greek Church Father and defender of the Trinity</note>: "Of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, there is one divinity, equal glory, and eternal majesty." In *The Christian Combat* <note>original: 'Agone christiano', referring to St. Augustine’s work 'De agone Christiano'</note>, **Augustine** appears to suggest that this dove was formed by God without the involvement of other doves, just as **CHRIST** was conceived in his mother's womb without male seed. However, this dove was not assumed into the unity of the person of the Holy Spirit in the same way that the humanity of **CHRIST** was unified [with his divine person].

### BOOK III.

Trinity: Sabellius <note>Sabellius (fl. 3rd century) was a priest who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not three distinct persons, but rather three "modes" or faces of a single person. This view, known as Modalism, was declared heretical.</note> posits in God the unity of the person, just as the unity of the essence; this is refuted when He says, "I and the Father are one." For, if the Father and the Son were one person, He would have said in the singular, "I am." Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336) taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father and of a different substance. This sparked the great Arian controversy which led to the Nicene Creed.</note>, on the contrary, posited a diversity of essences, just as there is of persons. ### BOOK III.

...ity <note>original: "tà"; likely completing "santità" (holiness) or "divinità" (divinity) from the previous page.</note>. **F.A.** To this I respond that the name "miracle" (according to St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian who defined miracles in his *Summa Theologiae* (I, q. 105).</note>) is derived from "wonder" [marvel]. Wonder arises when the effects are manifest, but the cause is hidden; just as occurs in the sight of an eclipse of the sun, where someone wonders, not knowing the cause, as Aristotle says in the first book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle famously argued that philosophy begins in wonder at things like the cycles of the moon and the sun.</note>. And the cause of a certain effect can be known to one person and unknown to another; therefore, an effect will be wonderful to one who does not understand it, but will not be wonderful to another. For example, a peasant marvels at the eclipse of the sun, but the astronomer <note>original: "Astrologo"; in the Renaissance, this term often encompassed both astronomy and astrology.</note> does not. 

A miracle is properly so called when it is "full of wonder"—that is, when its cause is absolutely unknown to everyone. Hence, those effects which are performed by God through secondary causes <note>In scholastic philosophy, "secondary causes" are the laws of nature or created beings through which God (the Primary Cause) usually works.</note> unknown to us, or outside the order of nature, are called miracles in an absolute sense. And because St. Thomas says in the First Part: "Not every power of created nature is known to us," therefore, when we see some unknown effect that does not follow the common order of nature, it is called a miracle, but not in an absolute sense <note>Here, "F.A." distinguishes between "relative miracles" (things we don't understand yet) and "absolute miracles" (things only God can do by overriding nature).</note>.

<summary>F.A. responds to the objection that miracles can be performed by sorcerers by defining what a true miracle is. Following Aquinas and Aristotle, he argues that while "wonder" depends on one's knowledge, a true miracle has a cause hidden from all of humanity and proceeds directly from God.</summary>

### BOOK III.

...but as for us. Thus, when demons perform an act through their natural power, that effect is called a miracle—not in the true sense, but according to our own judgment. This is because every power belonging to a created being in the universe acts like the power of a private individual within a city. 

Therefore, when a sorcerer performs an act through a pact agreed upon with a demon, it is done through a private contract. By contrast, **Divine justice** governs the entire universe just as the commonwealth <note>original: "republica"</note> governs a city. # BOOK III.

since God has promised to send him, [it cannot be that] before He sends him, He would have permitted anyone to reign in the world under the name of the one promised by Him, who would be a deceiver and a liar. Nor can it be, if God intended to send another, that He would permit any other deceiver to first come to precede him and reign under the name of the one promised by God Himself; for he would obstruct the true and legitimate future one. Therefore, it is necessary that he whom God has permitted to reign under the name of the one promised by God Himself, be that true promised one.

Therefore, it is impossible that **JESUS CHRIST**, crucified by the Jews, is not that true man whom God was to give to the world to <term>satisfy</term> <note>original: *sodisfar*; the theological doctrine of Atonement, where Christ pays the "debt" of human sin to divine justice</note> for sins. And **JESUS CHRIST** himself did nothing else but destroy sins, continually annulling them. And whatever he ordained, he ordained against sins; and all the ministers...
